items.definition: Everyone agreeing freely to something, every time. A clear no is a complete answer that needs no follow-up.
items.example: Consent has to be clear on both sides, and a no is always a complete answer.

items.definition: A metaphor for the meeting of people who are looking for a partner.
items.example: They talked about the dating market for an hour without saying anything about either of them.

items.definition: The group of people who are available to be chosen, counted as a group and not as individuals.
items.example: The supply was small where she lived, and the same people kept appearing.

items.definition: The group of wishes that the people looking are trying to satisfy.
items.example: The demand was for somebody who wanted a quiet life, and that changed who she met.

items.definition: The treatment of a person as a product that can be valued and exchanged.
items.example: The whole conversation turned her into a commodity, and she left the table.

items.definition: Acting in a planned way to produce a result, rather than acting in the way that comes naturally.
items.example: Strategic behaviour won him the interview; it did not make him better at the work.

items.definition: The number the market metaphor assigns to a person, as if it could be measured and compared.
items.example: He talked about his mate value instead of asking what she wanted.

items.definition: How many potential partners a person can actually meet, given where they live and how their life is arranged.
items.example: A thin market was the real problem: she kept meeting the same people.

items.definition: The capacity to say no without losing the chance of the thing you want.
items.example: Her bargaining power came from having other plans that week.

items.definition: The state in which too many options make the choosing harder instead of easier.
items.example: Too many profiles, and the choosing turned into work rather than pleasure.

items.definition: The effort a person pays to choose among the options available.
items.example: The price of choice was an evening spent reading instead of meeting anybody.

items.definition: Pairing with a person who is similar in background, position or values.
items.example: Homogamy is the word for the couple who grew up in the same kind of city.

items.definition: Pairing with a person who has less of a valued resource, such as income, education or position, than the chooser.
items.example: When one partner earns more, the pairing is hypogamy from one side and hypergamy from the other.

items.definition: Pairing with a person who has more of a valued resource, such as income, education or position, than the chooser.
items.example: Hypergamy names the direction of the pairing, and the direction can be read from either side.

items.definition: A situation where two people hold different views and are still talking. The other person is not automatically an enemy.
items.example: It was a disagreement about the schedule, not a fight.

items.definition: A disagreement that improves the decision being made and leaves the working relationship intact.
items.example: The meeting was tense but productive — it ended with a constructive disagreement and a clear next step.

items.definition: Soft words that mark your opinion as your opinion, such as 'maybe' or 'I could be wrong'. Useful in small doses.
items.example: A little hedging language keeps a sentence civil; too much of it hides your point.

items.definition: Giving the other side's position its strongest and most honest form before you argue against it.
items.example: Before you answer, steelman the other view in one sentence and see if it still convinces you.

items.definition: The part of a position that both people accept. Every polite disagreement starts by naming it.
items.example: Find the common ground first — both of you want this project to succeed.

items.definition: Listening to understand the other person's point, including checking your understanding, instead of waiting for your turn to speak.
items.example: Active listening means repeating their concern back before you answer it.

items.definition: The ability to stay with a strong feeling and still choose what you do next.
items.example: Her emotional regulation showed in the pause before she answered.

items.definition: The range of feeling intensity in which a person can hold the feeling and still think and speak plainly.
items.example: Outside his window of tolerance, every comment sounded like an accusation.

items.definition: The set of rules a relationship runs on although nobody has written them down or said them aloud.
items.example: Their unspoken contract said that the person who plans also drives.

items.definition: A belief about what will happen if you say nothing and do nothing about it.
items.example: Her expectation was that a refusal would come with an alternative.

items.definition: The raised state of the body that comes with a strong feeling, and that the other person can see.
items.example: Her activation was visible in the way she held the door open for too long.

items.definition: The way a person comes back down from activation and can choose again.
items.example: His recovery took the whole walk home, and the call waited until then.

items.definition: Putting a feeling into words as a way of getting the body back down.
items.example: The venting helped her settle, and the other person had heard none of it.

items.definition: Holding a feeling down so that nothing of it shows to the other person.
items.example: Her suppression looked like calm, and the calm was read as indifference.

items.definition: Changing the story you tell about an event so that the feeling loses its grip.
items.example: His reappraisal was honest: the message had been sent late, and it was not about her.

items.definition: Turning the same thought over again and again without moving towards an action.
items.example: Her rumination ran for days, and the argument she started was never the one she had been thinking about.

items.definition: The gap between what two people in a relationship each expect, when neither has said it aloud.
items.example: The expectation mismatch was about phone calls, and it had been there for months.

items.definition: A deliberate act of bringing the body back to a calm state before you act on a strong feeling.
items.example: Grounding gave her the pause she needed before she answered him.

items.definition: An acknowledgement that another person's feeling makes sense from their point of view.
items.example: Validation is not agreement: I can see why that hurt you, without changing his mind.

items.definition: An agreed action that puts a relationship back on track after something broke between two people.
items.example: Their repair was simple: they agreed to talk again the next evening.

items.definition: The capacity to stay in charge of your own reactions when the other person is difficult.
items.example: Her emotional maturity showed in the pause before she answered, not in the answer itself.

items.definition: The capacity to hold a reaction and choose when to act on it.
items.example: He used self-regulation to stay in the room instead of walking out.

items.definition: Reading what another person feels, and taking it seriously enough to act on it.
items.example: Her empathy showed in the question she asked instead of the advice she gave.

items.definition: The answer you owe for an act, to the people affected and to the law.
items.example: The mistake was hers, and the accountability was hers as well.

items.definition: The capacity to stay with a delay, a refusal or a mistake without making the other person pay for it.
items.example: Tolerance of frustration is what a good team leader buys with a calm answer on a Friday.

items.definition: The leaning towards acting before you have looked at what the act will do.
items.example: The message went out in impatience, and the impulsivity cost him the job.
